learn.title: Finding without searching
learn.body: Searching a list means looking at items one by one. A hash table tries to jump straight to where an item should be. It turns the key, such as a name or number, into an array index, then looks only there.

learn.title: Key to index
learn.body: A hash function takes a key and returns a number. Take that number modulo the table size, and you get a valid index. Using the same key always gives the same index, so storing and finding both go to the same slot.

learn.title: Keys to slots
learn.body: Three keys, a table of 10 slots. The remainder of dividing by 10 picks the slot.

learn.title: Finding 17
learn.body: The table has 10 slots, and 17 was stored using the rule above.
steps: Slot 7 holds 17, so it is found in one step, no matter how many items are stored

learn.body: The index is always at least 0 and below the table size, because a remainder is smaller than what you divide by.

questions.prompt: What does a hash table use to decide where an item goes?
questions.explanation: The same key must give the same place every time, so a function of the key is used.

questions.prompt: The table has 10 slots. Which slot does the key 38 use with `key % 10`?
Why take the hash modulo the table size?
choices: So the index fits inside the array
questions.explanation: A remainder is always between 0 and size minus 1.

questions.prompt: Looking up a key in a hash table starts by computing its \_\_.
questions.explanation: You hash the key, reduce it to an index, and look in that slot.

questions.prompt: Using the same key twice must give...
questions.explanation: Otherwise an item stored under a key could never be found again.

questions.prompt: A table with 10 slots holds 1000 items. A lookup by hash, when things go well, looks at...
questions.explanation: The hash points to the slot directly, so most of the other items are never examined.
